questions.q: What does showing up to your emotions mean?
a: Facing uncomfortable feelings instead of forcing a smile
Sharing every emotion with the people around you
Acting on whatever you feel in the moment
Replacing negative feelings with positive ones
questions.why: Lesson 1 says forced optimism cannot last, and even negative emotions can help if you face them directly.

questions.q: What did the Mills study find about genuine smiles?
a: Genuine smilers had better relationships and more satisfaction
Genuine smilers earned more money over their careers
Faked smiles predicted stronger emotional control
Smiling had no measurable effect on later life
questions.why: Lesson 1 says women whose smiles were genuine later reported better relationships, more emotional control and greater life satisfaction.

questions.q: Why does David suggest stepping out of your feelings?
a: Distance lets you observe emotions and choose your response
Distance makes difficult feelings disappear completely
Stepping out prevents you from feeling anything at all
Stepping out lets you avoid conversations about emotions
questions.why: Lesson 2 says noticing emotions without judging them creates space, so you can act in a more considered way.

questions.q: What distinguishes want-to goals from have-to goals?
a: Want-to goals come from your values, not outside pressure
Want-to goals are easier to achieve than have-to goals
Have-to goals always produce better long-term results
Have-to goals are set only by doctors and employers
questions.why: Lesson 3 says have-to goals are imposed by others, while want-to goals come from reflection on your own values.

questions.q: Which exercise helps clarify your want-to goals?
a: Writing a letter to your future self
Listing every goal your family expects of you
Comparing your salary with your peers'
Repeating your goals aloud each morning
questions.why: Lesson 3 suggests a letter to your future self, describing the person you hope to become in five, ten or fifteen years.
